In my election iu 1904 we expected some 5,300 votes to be polled and three weeks later about 4,300 votes were polled. So that it works both ways. I have no objection to holding the election on the same day. but I do not want the committee to accept a proposition which is not work-

able. I was looking at the hon. gentleman's amendment where the suggestion is made that the proclamation should he sent to the returning officer twenty-two clear days before nomination. That is sufficient time in the district of Yale-Cariboo. If the proclamation is in the hands of the returning officer twenty-two clear days before the general nomination day he has sufficient time to post this proclamation In every polling subdivision, as he is required to do hy law, but no more time. It will take him at least three weeks to post these proclamations in certain portions of the riding. Having put the proclamations up and the nominations being held, he is obliged to have the ballot boxes packed over the trails and to send returning officers in if there are none capable of doing the work, and it will take him three weeks more to prepare for the election after the nomination has been held. We tried it in three weeks at the last election, with the result that half of our deputy returning officers were not sworn in, because there was no justice of the peace within a hundred miles of some of the polling places. You have there, we will say, sixty days to be absolutely safe, from the time the proclamation reaches the hands of the returning officer before you can hold an election. It will take at least another week for the proclamation to go from Ottawa to the returning officer. That makes sixty-five or sixty-six days. If His Excellency the Governor General can dissolve this House find the proclamation can be Issued for an election sixty-six or seventy days before the election is held, I have no objection to a proposition of that kind, but I do not think it would be at all advisable or practicable that there should be a dissolution of this House granted, that the proclamation should be issued and that the whole country would have waited from sixty-six to seventy days before the election could take place because there are three or four constituencies in which it would be absolutely impossible to hold the election before that time.
How long after the last general election did the election take place in Yale-Cariboo?
Three weeks.
If it was only three weeks, then you did not have any sixty or seventy days after the issue of the writs.

The proclamation was issued on the 29th September, the election was held on November 3, and the election in Yale-Cariboo, being three weeks after that, it would make fifty-eight days. Although the returning officer gave three weeks for the last election, as a matter of fact, a number of the deputy returning officers in the more remote districts of Yale-Cariboo performed their duties on election day and were never sworn in.
We could not get a justice of the peace to swear them in. It is worse this year than it was four years ago, because, in the meantime, a great many people have gone in on the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and polls will have to be held in the Nechaco valley, at Fraser lake and in the Peace River country, where it will take six weeks to get the ballot boxes in. What is true of my constituency is true of Comox-Atlin, and the same difficulties will arise there. They make an exception in the Yukon. It takes more time to properly arrange for an election in Yale-Cariboo than in the Yukon district. As far as any advantage to be gained is concerned, I am not particular about that. Personally, I would much rather go on with the election on the date of the general election, because then you have your organization in working order. After the general election is over, and the Conservatives are defeated hopelessfy, your organization goes to pieces.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: May I submit to the right hon. leader of the House that it is now twelve o'clock, the Bill is all through except three sections and we might defer this discussion and continue it at a later time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Can we not
finish the Bill this evening?

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There are three sections still to be disposed of and when the Bill Is taken up again on another day-I understand it is not to be proceeded with tomorrow-we will dispose of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let us finish these amendments if you please.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Our leader has been obliged to leave to-night and his presence would facilitate matters. I do not think it would take long to dispose of the whole thing another day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How long ; two hours.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We could be expected to finish it in nine hours; it won't take long. The Speaker will be in the chair when probably most of the other amendments wfllbe moved.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We will take the word of my hon. friend that it will not take long.
Progress reported.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What business will be taken to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will take the Land Bill and some minor Bills and Committee of Supply.

Will the House sit after six o'clock to-morrow?

/

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will be guided by the wishes of the House in that matter.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at twelve o'clock (midnight).
